Primary Care Artificial Intelligence Research Surged but Implementation Evidence Remains Limited

Annual research output investigating artificial intelligence in primary health care expanded rapidly from 6 papers in 2015 to 220 in 2024, demonstrating consistent growth after 2018. However, an analysis of the evolving literature reveals that while investigator attention has broadened toward model evaluation and ethical governance, the surge in publication volume does not demonstrate routine clinical adoption or improved health outcomes in general practice.

To evaluate trends across primary care artificial intelligence literature, investigators searched the Web of Science Core Collection for records published between January 1, 2015, and October 19, 2025. Across an initial yield of 1,481 records, screening filtered out studies lacking specific primary care applications, those focusing solely on consumer or public health, and insufficiently relevant items. Using Python-based term lexicons, weighted scoring, and manual adjudication, researchers established a core analytical corpus of 1,123 articles and review articles.

A supplementary search identified 599 candidate papers to assess potential omissions caused by terminology variations. After applying screening criteria that excluded 457 records, 142 additional papers were integrated to assemble a 1,265-paper sensitivity corpus. This expanded sensitivity corpus was utilized specifically for keyword-frequency re-evaluations, co-occurrence mapping, and annual trend reruns, while 2025 was retained purely as an incomplete-year observation and excluded from complete-year growth comparisons.

Bibliographic coupling and thematic mapping revealed that primary health care artificial intelligence investigations have maintained a consistent core centered on machine learning, electronic health records, diagnostic support, and clinical screening. Over time, research themes underwent notable structural shifts. Methodological priorities expanded beyond initial model creation as model validation became increasingly common. While workflow integration and operational implementation remained visible throughout the analyzed decade, topics regarding governance and regulatory oversight emerged after 2018.

Between 2022 and 2024, academic attention turned substantially toward issues of fairness, algorithmic bias, and model explainability. Despite these thematic advancements across risk stratification, screening, and diagnostic support, the researchers emphasized a clear limitation in the evidence base. Expanding publication counts and thematic maturity reflect diversifying research priorities, but they do not confirm that these computational systems are widely deployed in routine practice or actively benefiting patient care.

Subject of Research: Bibliometric mapping of artificial intelligence research trends in primary health care

Article Title: Artificial intelligence in primary health care: a focused bibliometric mapping of research trends and changes in thematic attention (2015–2025)

Article References: Chen, Y., Li, T., & Zou, R. (2026). Artificial intelligence in primary health care: a focused bibliometric mapping of research trends and changes in thematic attention (2015–2025). Primary Health Care Research & Development, 27, Article e134. https://doi.org/10.1017/s1463423626102023

Keywords: artificial intelligence, primary health care, general practice, bibliometric analysis, machine learning, electronic health records, clinical decision support, diagnostic support, risk stratification, model validation, workflow optimization, algorithmic bias, fairness, explainability, health care governance, health informatics
